content:
Quick answer: A safe daily stretching routine for arthritis uses slow, gentle stretches held for about 10 to 30 seconds, without bouncing or forcing, within a comfortable range. Stretch after a short warm-up, ideally once or twice a day, and breathe normally. Mild tension is fine; sharp or increasing pain means ease off. Combine stretching with strengthening and walking.

Stiff joints and tight muscles are part of daily life for many people with arthritis. Gentle stretching helps keep joints moving through their range, eases stiffness and makes everyday tasks such as dressing, reaching and getting in and out of a car easier. This guide gives you a safe, 12-stretch routine that takes about 15 minutes, can be done seated or standing, and needs only a sturdy chair. It is general guidance. If you have had recent surgery, a joint replacement, or a physiotherapist has given you specific exercises, follow their advice first.

Why stretching helps with arthritis

  • Keeps joints moving. Joints that are not moved through their range tend to stiffen.
  • Eases muscle tightness around painful joints, which often tighten up to protect them.
  • Makes daily tasks easier, such as reaching a high shelf, putting on socks or looking over your shoulder when driving.
  • Prepares you for other activity such as walking or strengthening exercises.

The NHS physical activity guidelines for older adults recommend activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least two days a week, alongside regular moderate activity. NICE's osteoarthritis guideline (NG226) recommends exercise as a core treatment, tailored to the person. Stretching is one useful part of that mix, but it works best alongside strengthening and general activity such as walking, rather than on its own.

Safety rules before you start

  1. Warm up first. March on the spot or in your chair for 2 to 3 minutes, or stretch after a warm shower. Warm muscles stretch more comfortably.
  2. Go slowly. Move into each stretch gradually. Never bounce.
  3. Mild tension, not pain. You should feel a gentle pull in the muscle. Sharp, stabbing, burning or increasing pain means ease off.
  4. Hold, then release. Hold each stretch for around 10 to 30 seconds, building up over time. Repeat 2 or 3 times.
  5. Breathe normally. Do not hold your breath. Breathe out as you ease into the stretch.
  6. Stay steady. Use a sturdy chair without wheels, and hold on to a worktop or chair back for standing stretches.
  7. Use the 2-hour rule. A little extra aching is common when you start. If pain is noticeably worse for more than about 2 hours afterwards, or worse the next day, do fewer or smaller stretches next time.
  8. Respect joint replacements. After a hip or knee replacement, follow the movement advice from your surgical team or physiotherapist about which positions to avoid and for how long.

The 12-stretch routine

1. Neck turn

Sit tall with your feet flat on the floor. Slowly turn your head to look over your right shoulder as far as is comfortable. Hold for 10 to 20 seconds, then return to the middle and turn to the left. Keep your shoulders relaxed and chin level. Go gently if you have neck arthritis, and avoid tipping your head right back.

2. Neck side tilt

Sitting tall, gently tilt your right ear towards your right shoulder without lifting the shoulder, until you feel a stretch along the left side of your neck. Hold, then repeat on the other side. For a little more stretch, let the opposite arm hang down by your side.

3. Shoulder rolls and squeeze

Roll your shoulders slowly up, back and down five times. Then gently squeeze your shoulder blades together, as if holding a pencil between them, hold for 5 seconds and relax. Repeat five times. This helps counter rounded shoulders from sitting.

4. Chest opener

Sit forward on the chair. Clasp your hands behind your back, or hold the sides of the chair seat behind you. Gently draw your shoulders back and lift your chest until you feel a stretch across the front of your chest and shoulders. Hold for 15 to 30 seconds. If clasping hands is difficult, place your hands on your lower back instead.

5. Overhead reach

Lift one arm up towards the ceiling as far as is comfortable, keeping the elbow soft. You can lean very slightly to the opposite side to feel a stretch along your side. Hold, then lower slowly and swap. With a painful shoulder, lift only as high as is comfortable, or use your other hand to help support the arm.

6. Wrist and finger stretch

Hold one arm out in front, palm up. With your other hand, gently ease the fingers back towards you until you feel a stretch in the forearm. Hold for 10 to 15 seconds. Then turn the palm down and gently ease the hand down. Finish by making a loose fist, then spreading your fingers wide, five times. Our hand exercises guide has more for stiff hands.

7. Seated twist

Sit tall with feet flat. Cross your arms over your chest, or place your right hand on your left knee. Slowly turn your upper body to the left, keeping your hips facing forward. Hold for 10 to 20 seconds, return to the middle, then turn to the right. Keep the movement gentle if you have back pain or osteoporosis, and do not force the twist.

8. Seated hamstring stretch

Sit near the front edge of the chair. Straighten one leg out in front with the heel on the floor and toes pointing up. Keeping your back straight, lean forward slightly from the hips until you feel a stretch in the back of the thigh. Hold for 15 to 30 seconds and swap. Do not round your back to reach your toes.

9. Seated hip stretch

Sit tall. Rest your right ankle on your left knee, if you can, and gently press the right knee down while leaning slightly forward until you feel a stretch in the right buttock. Hold, then swap. If this is uncomfortable, or you have had a hip replacement, skip it or do a gentler version: sit with knees apart and slowly lean forward with a straight back. Follow your surgical team's advice about hip positions after a replacement.

10. Standing thigh stretch

Stand side-on to a worktop or sturdy chair and hold on. Bend one knee and bring the heel towards your bottom, holding your ankle, trouser leg or a towel looped around the ankle. Keep your knees close together and stand tall. Hold for 15 to 30 seconds, then swap. If balance or knee bending is difficult, do this lying on your side instead, or skip it.

11. Calf stretch

Face a worktop or wall and hold on. Step one foot back, keeping both feet pointing forwards and the back heel on the floor. Bend the front knee and lean gently forwards until you feel a stretch in the back calf. Hold for 15 to 30 seconds and swap.

12. Ankle circles and toe stretch

Sitting, lift one foot slightly and circle the ankle slowly five times each way. Then point the toes away and pull them back towards you five times. Finish by spreading your toes and curling them gently. Swap feet.

Short on time? The 5-minute version

  • Neck turn (1)
  • Shoulder rolls and squeeze (3)
  • Wrist and finger stretch (6)
  • Seated hamstring stretch (8)
  • Ankle circles (12)

When to stretch

  • Morning: after a warm shower, to ease stiffness. See our 15-minute morning routine.
  • Before activity: gentle movements to warm up before a walk.
  • After activity: a good time for longer holds, when muscles are warm.
  • Breaks from sitting: a couple of stretches every hour if you sit for long periods.
  • Evening: a gentle routine can help you wind down, but avoid vigorous exercise right before bed.

Adapting the routine

On flare days

Keep stretches small and gentle, and skip any that involve a hot, swollen joint. Instead, move that joint gently through a small, comfortable range a few times. Use cold on hot joints and warmth on stiff ones. Return to the full routine as the flare settles.

If balance is a concern

Do all stretches seated, or lying on a firm bed. Keep a phone within reach. Our exercise hub includes balance exercises, which help reduce the risk of falls.

If you have osteoporosis

Avoid forceful bending forward and twisting of the spine. Keep twists gentle and your back straight when leaning forward. Ask a physiotherapist for advice tailored to you.

After joint replacement

Follow your surgical team and physiotherapist's specific exercises and movement advice. Check with them before adding new stretches.

Hypermobility

If your joints are very flexible, focus on gentle movement and strengthening rather than pushing to the end of your range.

Building a routine that lasts

  • Link stretching to something you already do, such as after your morning cup of tea.
  • Start with fewer repetitions and shorter holds, and build up over a few weeks.
  • Note how stiff you feel before and after for a couple of weeks.
  • Add strengthening exercises on at least two days a week; for knees, see our knee exercises for osteoarthritis.
  • If you enjoy group exercise, look for chair-based, tai chi, yoga or Pilates classes for beginners or older adults, or try chair yoga.
  • Many areas allow self-referral to NHS physiotherapy for a personalised programme.

When to get medical help

  • Stop and get advice if a stretch causes sharp pain, a feeling of the joint giving way or locking, or new swelling.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E for a suddenly hot, red, swollen joint with fever, or if you injure yourself and cannot weight-bear.
  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness, or feeling faint or dizzy that does not settle when you stop.
  • See your GP or a physiotherapist if stiffness is getting worse, you have new joint swelling, morning stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes most days, or you are not sure which stretches are safe for you.

How long should I hold a stretch with arthritis?

Around 10 to 30 seconds is a good guide. Start with shorter holds if you are new to stretching or very stiff, and build up gradually. Repeat each stretch 2 or 3 times, and never bounce.

Is it OK to stretch if it hurts?

A gentle pulling feeling is normal. Sharp, stabbing, burning or increasing pain is not, so ease off or skip that stretch. A little extra aching afterwards is common at first; if pain is worse for more than about 2 hours, do less next time.

How often should I stretch with arthritis?

Once or twice a day suits many people, and even a short daily routine helps. The NHS recommends activities to improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least two days a week for older adults, alongside regular moderate activity.

Should I stretch during an arthritis flare?

Keep it very gentle. Skip stretches that load a hot, swollen joint and instead move it through a small, comfortable range a few times a day. Return to your normal routine gradually as the flare settles.

Is stretching enough exercise for arthritis?

No, stretching is one part. NICE recommends tailored exercise for osteoarthritis, which usually includes strengthening and general aerobic activity such as walking or swimming. Stretching helps flexibility and comfort, and works best alongside these.

Can I stretch after a hip or knee replacement?

Only as your surgical team and physiotherapist advise. There may be positions to avoid for a period after surgery, particularly after a hip replacement. Ask before adding stretches to the exercises you have been given.
